Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2016 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea

The government introduced the Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill to allow continued detention of high-risk terrorist offenders after their sentences expire, if a court deems them an unacceptable risk. The bill incorporates all 24 recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, has support from all states and territories, and enables Supreme Courts to issue continuing detention orders for up to three years with annual reviews.

The Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2016 was supported, introducing a continuing detention order regime for convicted terrorists judged an unacceptable risk, with safeguards including removal of treason from scope, access to legal representation, a 10-year sunset clause, and confirmation of constitutional validity from acting Solicitor-General Thomas Howe PSM QC. The government agreed to implement all 24 recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

The speaker supported the Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2016, which enables courts to order continued detention of high-risk terrorist offenders for up to three years after their sentence, with annual reviews and safeguards. He cited the case of Sevdet Ramadan Besim, who received a 10-year sentence for a planned Anzac Day attack, and praised the MyHack program run by Abdullah Alim.

Supported the Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2016 with amendments, and commended the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (PJCIS) for 24 recommendations. Raised concerns about the bill's lack of a framework for assessing terrorist reoffending risk, absence of robust expertise, and the need for preventive deradicalisation programs and ongoing monitoring.

The Criminal Code Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2016 establishes a framework for the continued detention of high-risk terrorist offenders after their custodial sentence if the Supreme Court finds they pose an unacceptable risk of committing a serious terrorist offence. The bill is modelled on existing state and territory post-sentence detention regimes, has been agreed to by all state and territory governments, and includes an implementation plan with a report to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security due by 30 June 2017.
